title: Factoring ax² + bx + c
short: Split the middle term using ac, then group.
trouble: Students factor as if a were 1, and never check by multiplying back out.

blocks.html: When the leading coefficient is not $1$, as in $6x^2 + 11x + 3$, guessing gets slow. The ac method turns it into something you already know: finding two numbers, followed by grouping.

Multiply out $(px + q)(rx + s) = prx^2 + psx + qrx + qs$. The two middle pieces, $psx$ and $qrx$, have coefficients whose product is $ps \cdot qr = pr \cdot qs$, which is $a \cdot c$, and whose sum is $b$. So: find two numbers that multiply to $ac$ and add to $b$, write the middle term as those two pieces, and the expression splits into two groups that share a binomial.

blocks.name: areamodel
blocks.cap: $6x^2 + 11x + 3 = (2x + 3)(3x + 1)$. The middle pieces are $2x$ and $9x$: they multiply to $18x^2$, and $18 = 6 \cdot 3 = ac$.

blocks.html: For $ax^2 + bx + c$: find two numbers with product $ac$ and sum $b$, split $bx$ into those two terms, then factor by grouping. Take out any GCF first.

blocks.title: The ac method
steps: $ac = 6 \cdot 3 = 18$. Two numbers with product $18$ and sum $11$: $2$ and $9$.

blocks.title: With a negative
steps: $ac = -60$. Numbers with product $-60$ and sum $-4$: $-10$ and $6$.

blocks.html: Factoring as if $a$ were $1$, for example writing $6x^2 + 11x + 3 = (x + 2)(x + 9)$ because $2 + 9 = 11$. That multiplies to $x^2 + 11x + 18$, not the original. Always multiply back: the first terms must give $ax^2$ and the last terms $c$.
